machine.shared: A development machine, with other work running at times; the A/B runs are alternated for that reason

build.tls: OpenSSL 3.6.5 (bundled, static: linux-ext-libs 1.26 in 7.28.0, 1.25 in 7.27.11); mbedTLS not built on this machine
build.note: CONFIG_DEBUG_TRACK_MEMORY is on (the .config of this machine): every allocation is tracked. A build without it does less work per allocation; that build was not measured here.

method.ab: Written on 2026-10-25, before the tag. 7.28.0 is the C code of main at d7c3e63e9 (the commits after it change no C of a library). It is measured against 7.27.11, the last release with a study; the releases between them (7.27.12 to 7.27.21, lite releases of the agent and the controlcenter) changed only c_authz.c in the kernel and are inside the same comparison. No figure got slower, so no tag between them had to be measured on its own. Each release built from a git worktree with the same .config and compiler, each with its OWN outputs_ext: 7.27.11 with the jansson of linux-ext-libs 1.25 (upstream v2.15.1 + patches/jansson/0001, atomic reference counts), 7.28.0 with linux-ext-libs 1.26 (jansson 2.15.1-yuneta.1, JANSSON_THREAD_SAFE_REFCOUNT=OFF); the other libraries are the same build. In each tree the kernel libraries, the modules, performance/c/ and the three ctest binaries were built; each tree runs its own benchmark sources, which differ only in the allocators given to jansson (7.28.0's take gbmem_get_json_allocators(), as every yuno of 7.28.0 does). The three benchmarks new in 7.28.0 (perf_ievent, perf_mqtt, perf_tr_treedb_read) were built in the 7.27.11 tree too, with the allocators of 7.27.11. The two binaries of each benchmark run in rotation, the order turned every round, with a sync and a 3 s pause before each run (1 s for the three ctest binaries and the read phase): 8 rounds; 24 for perf_tr_treedb, perf_timeranger2, the echoes, the BFF logins, perf_ievent and perf_mqtt; 48 for the append test (the test_topic_pkey_integer chain) and for the read phase; perf_rotatory and perf_tr_treedb_read 16. The two rotatory figures that measured slower were re-run in a controlled rotation of five binaries: 7.27.11, 7.28.0, and 7.28.0 relinked with 64, 128 and 192 bytes of pad before the libraries (the same machine code, moved). A third build, the code of 7.28.0 with the jansson of 7.27.11, ran in a three-way rotation (8 rounds, 12 for the appends and the reads) to split each gain between jansson and the rest. Mean +- standard deviation (median), t = the change over its standard error; |t| < 3 is noise. The treedb figures are CPU time of the process per operation.
method.tag_run: The absolute figures of 7.28.0 are its side of the A/B run: its C code (d7c3e63e9), built on 2026-10-25 on the machine of the earlier reports. The per-second benchmarks drop their first and last second; reads page by page are the FORWARD pass. The binary sizes are those of the yunos built from the main tree at the same C code, with the same .config.

story.title: Yuneta 7.28.0: twice the records, half the cost of an event
story.lead: 7.28.0 is a performance round over the whole C SDK, and Yuneta's own JSON library: jansson from github.com/artgins/jansson, upstream v2.15.1 with a series of Yuneta's commits. A yuno of 7.28.0 stores 1.9 times the records per second, reads 2.5 times as many, opens a treedb 17 times faster, and sends an event to another yuno and gets its answer twice as fast. The API is the same. Against 7.27.11, the last release with a study: 40 of 50 figures faster outside their noise, none slower.

hero.text: the records one yuno stores per second in a key-indexed topic: 422,850 appends/s, up from 225,745 in 7.27.11. The read of a store goes 2.5x: 549,780 records/s.

tiles: treedb: update a node and save it
story.ab_sub: Each benchmark built from the tree of each release (7.27.11 and 7.28.0, each with its own jansson), the binaries run in rotation: 8 rounds, 24 for the treedb writes, the store open, the echoes, the BFF logins, the inter-yuno events and MQTT, 48 for the appends and the read path, 16 for the treedb reads and the rotatory. A change inside its whisker is noise. Everything is on one axis: the change of the time an operation takes.
story.prices_sub: What got slower, how much, in which release, and what it buys.
story.no_prices: None. Two figures of the rotatory measured slower in the rotation of the study, the log record +1.0% (t = 3.4) and the audit record with its retention +1.8% (t = 8.0). The rotatory is the same code in both releases. In a controlled rotation, the same 7.28.0 moved by 64, 128 and 192 bytes measured the log record from +0.3% to +1.45% and the audit record with retention from +0.06% to +2.2% against 7.27.11: code placement, not code. The event loop alone (perf_yev_ping_pong, no gobj, no json) stays where it was, +0.5% (t = 1.2): the gain is in the layers above it.
story.abs_sub: Absolute figures of the 7.28.0 build (its C code: d7c3e63e9), measured on 2026-10-25, before the tag, on the laptop above, as its side of the A/B run: one process, one core for the event loop (Yuneta scales by running one yuno per core). Mean of the rounds; the spread and the rounds are in the table at the end.

split.title: Where the gain comes from
split.sub: A third build ran in the same rotation: the C code of 7.28.0 with the jansson of 7.27.11. Its bar is between the two releases: what is left of the gain is jansson's. timeranger2 owes most of its gain to jansson, because a record is a json that is dumped when it is written and parsed when it is read. The treedb and the network owe most of theirs to the rest of the round: the subscriptions read from a C record, no EV_STATE_CHANGED that nobody sees, the treedb open of the newest record of a key, the indexed hooks, a websocket frame in one write. The three builds ran 8 rounds (12 for the appends and the reads), so their figures differ a little from the A/B above. The rest of the round includes jansson's allocators without zeroing (gbmem_get_json_allocators()), and 7.27.12 to 7.27.21 (only c_authz.c changed in the kernel).
split.middle_label: the code of 7.28.0 with the jansson of 7.27.11

entries.label: Appends per second
entries.text: jansson's share of the gain: 86%. The dump of a record gathered in a buffer, a short string in one block.

entries.label: Records read, iterator
entries.text: jansson's share: 86%. The lexer reads runs of plain bytes; a string token has no allocation of its own.

entries.label: Page of 100 rows, master
entries.text: jansson's share: 76%. A page is parsed records.

entries.label: Reopen the treedb
entries.text: jansson's share: 1%. The open reads the newest record of each key only and rebuilds the hooks indexed.

entries.label: Update a node and save it
entries.text: jansson's share: 24%. The columns of a topic read once while its cols is the same json; no EV_STATE_CHANGED nobody sees.

entries.label: Views as json text
entries.text: jansson's share: 91%. A view dumped to json text is jansson's dump.

entries.label: TCP echo, gobj stack
entries.text: jansson's share: 6%. The publications read their subscriptions from a C record; an event nobody would see is not built.

entries.label: TLS echo, gobj stack
entries.text: jansson's share: 10%. Same as the TCP echo; an OpenSSL read takes a gbuffer of the size it read.

entries.label: Inter-yuno events
entries.text: jansson's share: 43%. Each round trip parses one frame and dumps one; the websocket frame goes in one write and is unmasked in place.

entries.label: MQTT QoS 0
entries.text: jansson's share: 13%. Mostly the gobj layer: the broker's publications and subscriptions.

entries.label: OAuth2 BFF logins
entries.text: jansson's share: 62%. An HTTP request and its json answer per login.
